Thinking is Fun!

0–8 minutes · Ungraded opening

Your best friend cheats in a competition and wins. Should you report them, even if nobody will ever find out?

Write 2–3 sentences explaining your answer and why. After that, discussion only.

Different ways to think

Loyalty: Friendship creates responsibilities. Could helping your friend admit the truth be an act of loyalty?

Fairness and duty: Other competitors followed the rules. Would you accept the same choice if the winner were a stranger?

Consequences: Consider who benefits or gets hurt, now and later.

Character: What kind of friend and person do you want to become?

  1. Does your answer change if the prize is only a candy bar?
  2. What if the prize is a college scholarship?
  3. Would giving your friend a chance to confess change your responsibility?
  4. Should loyalty change what counts as fair?

Final twist

What if your friend cheated because everyone else was cheating?

No additional writing.

What turns numbers into power?

8–20 minutes · Discuss together

Hypothetical: One student asks the principal to change an unpopular school policy. Now imagine the entire tenth grade organizes and makes the same request.

What changes? What could make the group hard to ignore? Does a larger group guarantee success?

Watch: A Bug’s Life — Hopper’s grain demonstration

If the ants already outnumber the grasshoppers, why don’t they already have the power?

Workers can organize

A union lets workers act together. Through collective bargaining, representatives negotiate over pay, hours, and conditions. A strike adds pressure by withholding labor the employer needs.

One worker asks. A union negotiates together. Workers who strike collectively stop production.

Can you afford to keep striking?

Hypothetical: You support your coworkers’ demands, but your family needs your next paycheck. What would make joining possible? What might make you return to work?

Ask what each side loses each day and who can wait longer. Organization, solidarity, savings, replacement workers, and government authority affect bargaining power.

Where the movie analogy has limits

The movie creates clear villains. Historical employers and workers had varied circumstances and motives. We need evidence to evaluate their claims. A principal hearing a request also differs from an employer losing production.

Why did workers strike?

Reason for strikingPossible grievance
WagesPay cuts or earnings that did not cover living expenses
HoursLong workdays and workweeks
ConditionsUnsafe or unhealthy work
Security and rulesLayoffs, irregular employment, fines, or unfair treatment
Union recognitionRefusal to negotiate with a union or retaliation for organizing

Cartoon transfer: The Protectors of Our Industries

Bernhard Gillam, Puck, February 7, 1883. This predates Pullman. “Protection” also alludes to tariffs, defended as a way to protect American industry and jobs. First inspect the image independently.

Reading the small lettering

The bags include industrialists’ names and “millions.” Wage signs include cloth workers averaging $9 a week and linen workers averaging $11 a week. The water is labeled “hard times.” These are the cartoon’s labels, not independently verified wage data.

Pullman: a local dispute becomes a national boycott

38–62 minutes · Background and primary sources

The Pullman Company built railway passenger cars near Chicago and owned a planned town with rental housing. Factory jobs offered wages, and the town offered services and housing. Company control also limited workers’ influence over important parts of daily life.

After the depression of 1893 reduced orders, Pullman reduced wages without corresponding rent reductions. Workers sought concessions. The factory strike began May 11, 1894.

  1. Factory workers strike: Pullman’s manufacturing work stops.
  2. Railway workers join a boycott: American Railway Union members refuse to handle Pullman cars on other companies’ railroads.
  3. Disruption spreads: The dispute affects rail traffic, mail, and interstate commerce.

Factory workers and railway workers were different groups. The ARU excluded Black workers from membership, limiting who could participate in this organization.

A. Jennie Curtis, worker and union leader

Curtis was a seamstress and president of ARU local 269. She testified under oath on August 16, 1894, after the conflict.

We went there and asked, as the men did, for more wages; we were cut lower than any of the men’s departments throughout the works; in 1893 we were able to make 22 cents per hour, or $2.25 per day, in my department, and on the day of the strike we could only earn, on an average, working as hard as we possibly could, from 70 to 80 cents a day.

Selected answer to question 10. Her department’s experience does not establish the pay reduction for every Pullman worker.

B. Pullman Company statement

The company explained the decline in orders and defended its decisions. Its statement reports Pullman speaking “in substance,” rather than providing a verbatim recording.

Negotitions with intending purchasers of railway equipment...were stopped by them, orders already given by others were canceled, and we were obliged to lay off, as you are aware, a large number of men in every department, so that by November 1, 1893, there were only about 2,000 men in all departments, or about one-third the normal number.
The renting of the dwellings and the employment of workmen at Pullman are in no way tied together...

Selected passages, commission report pp. 578–581. Original spelling “Negotitions” retained. Ellipses mark omissions.

Who could change the outcome?

62–73 minutes · Discuss the evidence

Look first: What can you see? What does the photograph leave unanswered about orders, motives, or actions?

DevelopmentEffect on bargaining power
The railway boycott disrupted trafficCollective action increased pressure beyond the factory.
Railroad managers coordinated and hired replacement workersEmployers had resources and alternatives to striking workers.
A federal court issued an injunction; federal marshals and troops intervenedGovernment officials cited mail delivery, interstate commerce, and enforcement of court orders. Intervention weakened the boycott.
Union leaders faced arrest and broader strike support failed to materializeThe boycott collapsed in mid-July. Workers did not secure the concessions they sought.

Violence occurred during the wider conflict. Do not assume everyone in crowds was a striker or every striker engaged in violence.

Government and business

In major Gilded Age labor disputes, courts and government authorities frequently acted in ways that strengthened employers and weakened strikes. Officials did not always agree: Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld opposed President Cleveland’s deployment of federal troops.

A commission checks the claims

While reducing wages, the company made no reduction in rents.

The U.S. Strike Commission also challenged the claim that housing and employment were fully separate: workers feared losing employment if they lived elsewhere. This was an investigative finding, not a guarantee of complete neutrality.

Discuss: Which action changed the workers’ alternatives most? Explain its mechanism, not just which side benefited.

Why strike? Why win or lose?

73–85 minutes writing · 85–94 flexible time and debrief · 94–100 submit

Reasons for striking: the grievances that made workers seek change.

Power to win: the resources, alternatives, cooperation, and authority that shaped the outcome.

Optional paragraph support

Workers struck because ___. Source ___ shows ___. Organizing increased their power by ___. However, ___ limited that power. Government action ___ changed the outcome because ___. This helps explain why ___.

Debrief

Numbers can create leverage when people organize and sustain action. Employers’ alternatives and government authority can counter that leverage. Pullman’s defeat does not show that all unions always failed, and the long-term graphs alone cannot show how much unions caused improvement.
